goal:
Make `slugify` in `src/slugify.js` turn Latin letters with diacritics into plain ASCII: `slugify("Crème Brûlée")` returns `"creme-brulee"` and `slugify("Łódź")` returns `"lodz"`.

This covers every Latin letter, not only those Unicode can split into a base letter and an accent: letters with a stroke and ligatures take their usual ASCII spelling (for example `ø` → `o`, `æ` → `ae`, `ß` → `ss`). Accents count whether the title writes them precomposed or as separate combining marks after the letter.

Keep everything that works today. In particular, letters of other scripts stay exactly as they are: `slugify` keeps Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, and every other script unchanged, apart from lower case.

constraints: Change as few files as possible.
Delete or simplify existing code before you add code.
Write a failing test that reproduces the problem before you change any source file.

+ * Turns a title into a URL slug: lower case, transliterate Latin accents, and

 export function slugify(title) {

challengers.defect: Unicode normalization and combining-mark removal apply to every script, altering non-Latin letters that should remain unchanged.

candidates.approach: Implement a Latin-only normalization helper in src/slugify.js. Identify Latin letters together with their following combining marks, decompose those sequences, remove their accents, and apply a comprehensive fallback mapping for Latin letters that normalization cannot convert to ASCII, including ł, ø, æ, and ß. Leave non-Latin sequences untouched, then retain the existing lowercasing, separator collapsing, and edge trimming. Restricting normalization and mark removal to Latin sequences prevents changes to Greek, Cyrillic, Japanese, or other scripts.
candidates.firstStep: Add regression tests covering the two requested examples, non-decomposing Latin letters, decomposed Latin accents, and unchanged non-Latin behavior; then inventory the fallback mappings needed beyond Unicode decomposition.

candidates.approach: Generate a complete Latin-to-ASCII lookup table at build or development time from a pinned Unicode inventory and reviewed transliteration data. At runtime, slugify performs direct code-point substitutions without normalizing the input, consumes combining accents following Latin letters, and leaves all other letters unchanged before applying its existing formatting pipeline. Commit the generated table and its generator so coverage is reproducible and Unicode upgrades can be reviewed explicitly.
candidates.firstStep: Create a generator prototype that enumerates Unicode Latin letters and reports which lack an approved ASCII mapping, including letters whose conventional spelling requires multiple characters.

candidates.approach: Use an existing transliteration dependency behind a strictly Latin-only adapter. Pass only Latin letters and their attached combining marks to the library, preserve every non-Latin segment verbatim, and feed the reconstructed title through the existing slug formatting logic. This delegates mapping maintenance but requires an exhaustive coverage audit: generic transliteration libraries may alter other scripts, miss obscure Latin letters, or choose spellings different from the required conventions.
candidates.firstStep: Inspect the project's dependency and runtime constraints, then evaluate candidate libraries against a Unicode-wide Latin-letter corpus and explicit examples such as ł, ø, æ, and ß.

candidates.approach: Implement an explicit, ordered regex rewrite pipeline rather than normalization or per-character lookup. Group Latin variants by their ASCII spelling, replace each group with its target letter or sequence, and remove combining marks only when they follow a recognized Latin letter. Keep the current final slug cleanup unchanged. This dependency-free approach is likely less maintainable than the alternatives, but offers a different mechanism with directly inspectable replacement rules; comprehensive Unicode coverage would require extensive groups and validation.
candidates.firstStep: Prototype replacement groups for accented vowels, stroked letters, and ligatures, then build an inventory test that identifies every Latin letter not covered by those rules.
